passages: [prose] Among freshwater macroinvertebrates, Odonata (Insecta) are a good model taxon for exploring the effects of climate warming on freshwater biodiversity because (1) they originated in the tropics, which implies tolerance to high temperatures; (2) adults present high morphological differentiation across species, which facilitates capture, identification and recording; (3) they occur with medium to high local abundances and are present in almost all freshwater habitats, with high species turnover due to larval and adult preferences in habitat use and evident niche partition among species; (4) they present high phenotypic variability, both within and between species, in traits pre-sumably involved in adaptation to climate warming, such as emergence and duration of flight season; and (5) there is a large and wellknown body of historical research, including extensive recording and rich historical datasets from citizen science projects (Corser et al., 2014; Hassall & Thompson, 2008; Termaat et al., 2019).

[prose] The first fPCA axis of the functional space (Figure 4a; Supporting information S8) explained 20.85% of the total variability, whereas the second and third axes explained respectively 13.62% and 10.94%. The trait categories most correlated to the first axis were semivoltinism (NC0) together with the opposite patterns of behaviour fliers (FBF) versus perchers (FBP), and the water quality oligotrophic (WO) versus eutrophic (WE). The second axis was mostly related with the opposite directions of absence (DN) versus presence (DY) of egg diapause. The trait categories most correlated with axes (>0.6) were selected (Supporting information S9).

Ellipses cluster the species belonging to the same category of range-shift responses, each colour and letters corresponding to a different range-shift response as in Figures 1a and 2; (b) arrows represent the most weighted trait categories for principal components 1 and 2 on fPCA (see trait abbreviation in Supporting information S2); (c) distribution of species by discriminant analysis (DA) space; (d) significant traits that discriminated between the categories of range-shift responses in DA. From left to right and from up to down: flight season (FS); range margins (R); habitat type (H); oviposition habitat (O); river zonation (A); vegetation at the breeding site (V); and voltinism (NC). The categories within a trait are depicted in the same colour.

[prose] 1. Climate change has the potential to modify habitat characteristics and, consequently, induce species responses to ongoing environmental changes. Functional traits determine both if a species can persist and maintain stable population sizes in particular ecological conditions, and its capacity to disperse to more favourable habitats. 2. Given that functional traits evolve over time, one could expect closely related species to show similar responses to climate change, which should identify vulnerable lineages. Alternatively, species-specific functional traits may anticipate species responses to climate change, and therefore, trait composition should be a strong predictor. 3. We compiled a comprehensive dataset of functional traits of 84 Iberian and Moroccan odonates species and built a phylogenetic tree to determine if dissimilarity of traits and phylogenetic relatedness are relevant to better discriminate species range-shift responses to climate change. 4. Current climatic conditions were described by 19 bioclimatic variables based on temperature and rainfall values. These variables were downloaded from [worldclim.org](http://worldclim.org) at 30 arc-second resolution based on monthly averages for the period 1970–2000. Bioclimatic variables are commonly used in SDMs for predicting species ranges and were originally created to generate more biologically meaningful variables than traditional environmental metrics such as mean temperature and pre-cipitation (O’Donnell & Ignizio, 2012).
